speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Home Team enjoys high levels of trust and confidence amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Principally, it is because our Home Team continues to deliver on the promise to make Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As parliamentarians, we need to ensure that our Home Team is provided with sufficient resources and legislative levers so that they will be in a good position to deliver on their mission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I will focus on two areas: first, providing better support to the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD), our premier white-collar crime buster, in the fight against complex white-collar crime; and second, reviewing the effect of the death penalty as a deterrent against drug trafficking, murder and other serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the first topic, we have seen a significant increase in complex white-collar crime cases in Singapore which are being investigated by the CAD.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some of these cases have been unearthed because of the economic downturn caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, if not for the pandemic, the fraudulent conduct could have carried on without detection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Needless to say, such cases affect the reputation of Singapore and her financial system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These perpetrators must be dealt with firmly by the law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But one thing astonishes me – what makes these people think that they can get away with their offending conduct in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The scale and nature of these crimes show that this is daylight robbery, not a thief in the night.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: People convicted of serious white-collar crimes are imposed deterrent sentences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But why do these crimes worth several billion dollars still happen with some regularity on our shores?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that one issue we have not yet nailed is detection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A good number of these fraudsters think that their acts will not be detected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is there any basis for this sort of thinking?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If there is, we better make sure that we address this expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need a framework that will enable white-collar crimes to be detected as early as possible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These persons must get the message that if they do the crime, they will be detected and will have to pay a high price.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that there are already established strategies, such as leveraging data analytics, to process suspicious transaction reports, cash movement reports, cash transaction reports by institutions and individuals in Singapore, as well as deepening of intelligence capability through partnerships.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Other financial centres, such as the US and UK, have such legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have made the same suggestion in the past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reality is that the white-collar crime criminals obviously commit their acts in secrecy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we see in the open is not robbery but a legitimate front.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The real underbelly can only be exposed through insiders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Insiders are not likely to volunteer information unless their interests are protected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I know this is a separate matter from providing incentives but, in a risk-benefit calculus, the benefit may not be just mere protection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are incentivised by way of rewards, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another suggestion I have is to review the role of external auditors in order that they are in a better position to detect fraud in companies and report the matter to CAD.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members may be familiar with the German Parliament’s investigation into the shortcomings of the Wirecard’s auditors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There must be better alignment between the auditor’s role currently and the investing public’s expectations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, we need to decisively tackle the problem of resourcing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggest we beef up manpower internally and be more open to engaging other experts from the outside.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: CAD is operating in a challenging environment on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Despite that, it is doing a very good job in bringing offenders of complex white-collar crimes to book.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As legislators, we need to ensure that CAD is sufficiently resourced so that investigations into complex white-collar crime are conducted fully and with due dispatch.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The faster the culprits are prosecuted, the stronger the message of deterrence will be against like-minded offenders in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is the Government’s responsibility to ensure adequate resourcing to deal with criminality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have heard laments about problems in recruiting people as IOs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, this is not an answer I accept.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move on to the second point of my speech, which deals with the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government’s approach has resulted in Singapore being one of the safest places in the world – something that is deeply valued by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Two significant changes to the law had happened since 2013.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, the death penalty would only be imposed as a mandatory sentence for intentional murder.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the other forms of murder, the Court has a discretion to impose either the death penalty or life imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Of the remaining 22, eight persons were imposed with life imprisonment on the basis that they were suffering from an abnormality of mind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Court imposed the death penalty on 14 persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The number of persons subjected to the mandatory death sentence has been reduced significantly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Nonetheless, there could be a watering down of the deterrent effect of the death penalty for drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, therefore, ask whether there has been any deterioration on the part of the Home Team’s ability to keep our drug situation under check.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If there is no deterioration, may I ask whether the Government is prepared to consider extending the issuance of certificates of substantial assistance to cover cases where drug couriers whose death penalties have been affirmed on appeal?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Most essentially, Singaporeans must continue to be convinced that the retention of the death penalty is essential for the Home Team to do its job.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fact that most Singaporeans agreed in the past does not mean that their views may not change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Outside Singapore, more and more jurisdictions have abolished the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singaporeans’ opinions can be shaped by these developments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Has there been any recent survey to measure Singaporean support?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our officers already enjoy the trust of Singaporeans from arresting the trend of increasing white-collar crime to deterring serious crimes, such as drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our officers must be well-resourced, supported and adequately compensated so as to ensure that we continue to attract the best and the brightest to take on the heavy task of keeping us safe.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It has been a part of criminal justice systems for thousands of years and references to it can be found in the Code of Hammurabi in Babylon more than 3,000 years ago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is usually reserved for the most serious of offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the last 50 to 60 years though, a number of countries, including most of Europe, have abolished the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are various groups lobbying for its abolition in many parts of the world, including in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is usually based on humanitarian grounds because, despite the seriousness of the crime involved, when one looks at the world from the perspective of the offender, there is usually a sad story involved as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has done well in keeping these serious crimes under control.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our rates of murder, kidnapping and firearm use are extremely low, with the latter two offences being very rare.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That drug trafficking is more rampant than the other serious crimes is not surprising because there are well-financed organised syndicates running this business.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How does Singapore compare with countries that do not impose the death penalty in relation to these serious crimes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, in some of our laws, the Government has sweeping powers over many activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the Home Affairs Minister’s FICA round-up speech, he said if the CPIB hypothetically “wants to investigate the Prime Minister, there is a higher authority they report to." I would like to return to one question I raised during that debate, which is, who checks the checkers, and specifically in relation to foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The world is changing and geopolitical tensions are ratcheting up to levels that have not been seen in recent memory.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Ministers, including the Home Affairs Minister and Prime Minister himself, would be extremely high-value targets for foreign interference, particularly given what some might say is Singapore’s significant role in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does it reside with the CPIB, which is what the Home Affairs Minister’s reply suggested?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If so, does the CPIB proactively assess risks of foreign interference against Ministers or does it act only reactively, if complaints are lodged?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are there officers in the CPIB with the necessary skills and expertise to investigate possible foreign interference?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of an Ombudsman would create investigative resources behind a legitimate institutional check that would be seen to be legitimate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the current climate, there is more of a need for this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While I accept that there is a need for in-prison disincentives against dangerous behaviours, in my opinion, there is too little independent oversight in this process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Institutional Discipline Advisory Committee reviews the recommended strokes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can reform with a judicial element be studied, so we have a greater oversight mechanism?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is important in respect of caning, which is a harsh punishment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not alleging that this is the case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I would like to ask the Government if this is a current practice and, if so, would the Government consider stopping it, as it is unnecessary and seems of questionable rehabilitative value, to put it mildly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But they are also centres of hope and second chances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Over several decades, our officers of the Singapore Prison Service, known as Captains of Lives, had been working assiduously to turn our prisons into rehabilitation centres for inmates – to reform and reintegrate into society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This House has heard about the good work that the Singapore Prison Service, Yellow Ribbon Singapore and their partners do in rehabilitating prisoners in January 2022 when the hon Minister of State Faishal Ibrahim, moved amendments to the Prisons Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As hon Members may recall, the amendments introduced the Employment Preparation Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Under this scheme, inmates were allowed an opportunity to undergo skills training in the community so that they will be able to get good jobs upon their release.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In his speech, the hon Minister of State recounted the important steps taken by the Singapore Prison Service over almost four decades to help inmates in their journey of rehabilitation and reintegration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These rates are among the lowest in the world, with only a few countries such as Norway, doing better than Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The question arises as to what more should be done to help our inmates reform and lower recidivism even further.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One in five slipping back into a life of crime is still one too many.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Over time, our prison population is gradually reducing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: From my own calculations, I worked out the Singapore prison population rate as at 2020, to be 163 per 100,000.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This compares with 212 per 100,000 across the Causeway in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, there are states with lower figures than ours.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I cite three:	Hong Kong's rate is 96 per 100,000; South Korea's is 105 per 100,000; and England's rate is 132 per 100,000.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To be fair, when I looked at our prison population figures, I noted that the main driver is actually those who have committed drug offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Although this tough stance means that more people will be jailed or detained in drug rehabilitation centres (DRCs), I support this as our way of dealing with this scourge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It seems to me, therefore, to lower recidivism in a more decisive way, we will have to focus even more on the rehabilitation and aftercare programmes for these drug offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is, obviously, not easy, but we are fortunate that, in Singapore, SPS, CNB and its partners have been doing excellent work on this front for a long time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One suggestion I have is to carefully monitor the company that drug offenders keep during the time that they are subject to drug supervision orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I came across a case of an ex-inmate who, when reporting for urine test, reconnected with old friends who were also reporting for urine tests and thereafter, started committing crime together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It sounds perhaps too much like a surveillance state to require that we keep tabs on who such supervisees meet or constrain them from mixing around with more hardened offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have in mind something more like using the good to crowd out the bad.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Occupy their time and energies with new and interesting options.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Motivating inmates, providing them with the structural and emotional support to reform from within themselves, giving them opportunities to learn new skills and acquire knowledge, emplacing them in decent jobs and helping them reintegrate into their families and societies are important steps to lower recividism amongst our inmates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I look forward to hearing from the hon Minister on his plans to further cut the recividism rate and reduce our prison population.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the Institute of Policy Studies' 2020 instalment of the World Values Survey found that our Courts and the Singapore Police Force enjoyed admirably higher levels of confidence, compared to our Government and Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, the low level of crime in Singapore is a key indicator of the success that law enforcement has achieved.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will be speaking on the role of the community in building a holistic criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This warrants some pondering as to why the rate of reoffending goes up steeply after the first two years of being released.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I know that, as had been debated in Parliament last year when the Singapore Prisons Act was amended, there are significant Government programmes for ex-offenders immediately before and immediately after release.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These include the Employment Preparation Scheme and a community-based programme.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, in order for us to keep the likelihood of reoffending low, we need to make sure that the community plays its part in conjunction with Government programmes and importantly, after Government programmes have completed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Some community initiatives include the Singapore After-Care Association's befriending programme and the HCSA Highpoint Halfway House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, I would like to ask the Minister what other efforts has MHA made to look at the criminal justice system, from a holistic perspective, to prevent individuals from offending or re-offending.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, and based on my experience as a volunteer probono lawyer, I have noticed that there are many drug offence-related re-offenders.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This appears to be corroborated by a 2018 paper by Stephanie Chok at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy on drug offenders in Singapore that the recidivism rates for drug offenders has been consistently higher than overall recidivism rates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the figures quoted by Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua yesterday with regard to the noticeable rise in the number of youth drug abusers from 2016 to 2019 are troubling.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have two questions as regards preventing drug offences in the first place and reducing the likelihood of re-offending.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My first question is with regard to MHA and CNB's collaboration with the community in the fight against drugs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: An example is a partnership between PERSES, the Sepaktakraw Federation of Singapore, and the Dadah Itu Haram campaign.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As Senior Minister of State Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim has said about this collaboration, it was a step showing how the rest of the sports community could join in the anti-drug effort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, could the Minister update on MHA's efforts in spreading the anti-drug message to various communities and the impact it had made thus far?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My second question is with regard to the death penalty for drug offences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another study in 2018, this time on a sample of non-Singaporeans who were likely to visit Singapore came to similar conclusions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Shanmugam had also mentioned in the House in October 2020 that there was evidence that knowledge of the death penalty led to a reduction in the amount of drugs trafficked.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister said then, these and other surveys quite clearly show that there is majority public support for the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On this, would the Minister be able to give a comparative view, that is, how Singapore compares with other countries that do not impose the death penalty for drug trafficking offences?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On my final point, Madam, part of the community effort in bolstering our criminal justice system is ensuring that the public support for law enforcement that I mentioned at the start of my speech is not eroded.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, all of us have a part to play.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, we must make sure that we do not make any allegations about law enforcement without being absolutely sure of the factual basis of these allegations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is incumbent on the authorities as well to swiftly crush even rumours of any impropriety if they are untrue.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Equally, MHA and the Police must continue to be transparent about disciplinary cases and make these public.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This gives confidence that the system of internal checks works and that errant officers are taken to task.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, Madam, we must also speak up in support of our officers when they do well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will end, Madam, with a quote from a LinkedIn post by Ms Sadhana Rai, a criminal defence lawyer at the Law Society's Criminal Legal Aid Scheme.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: She wrote, "In my experience as a defence counsel..." – and we should know that defence counsel are opposite the AGC and opposite the investigation officers (IOs) in the Court setting – "...I have come across some hardworking, sensitive and professional investigation officers who go out of their way to ensure that complainants are safe, comfortable and emotionally supported.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These officers accompany complainants to Court, sit through proceedings, speak to the complainants on breaks to make sure they are doing alright and more.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We are all important parts in a system that aims to uphold and deliver justice."

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I also echo hon Member Zhulkarnain bin Abdul Rahim's suggestion to call ex-offenders the "overcomers" – having overcomed the difficulties of the past.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One of the things inmates worry about is whether they can get a job after prison and whether they can have the right skills to keep up with the demands of the job.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I also understand that inmates can also be matched with specific jobs after they complete their courses with compatible employers who are prepared to give them a chance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is a great initiative that allows inmates to receive targeted and industry-specific skills training.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister share what progress has been made on improving the job search process for ex-offenders and how can progressive and inclusive human resource practices towards ex-offenders be recognised, incentivised and encouraged further?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are now commonplace in our neighbourhoods and public areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Feedback from the Police officers have also been positive, with some commenting that these cameras have doubled their effectiveness in solving crimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Police Cameras have improved Singapore's safety and security while improving our officers' productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, camera technology and analytics have improved significantly since 2012.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the Ministry balance crime-solving with privacy?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will the footages be used to tackle social issues, such as illegal smoking?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I recall the move to install Police Cameras in the access points of all HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Following this, the number of loan shark harassment cases had reduced significantly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: And I am aware of at least one murder case where the Police identified and arrested the suspect based on the footage and cameras.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We see more signs of speed cameras and traffic light cameras, which, in turn, generally, encourage compliance, so much so that, whenever there is trouble, people ask for more cameras to be installed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I had raised previously in this House that I receive regular complaints from residents in relation to speeding at Woodlands Avenue 5 and the initial response was that the Police would send more patrols.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But residents were wondering why cameras were not used instead of patrols.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Singapore transforms to fulfil its vision to be a Smart Nation, the role of data has come increasingly to the forefront.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With increasing technological capability, the ability to collect and handle a large volume of data and analyse it is now possible, leading to the ability to make predictions and anticipate events and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the realm of public safety and security, this is vital, especially during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While machine learning and various software are currently available, the possibility of assessing trends in location, type of crime and likelihoods of criminal activity can allow the Home Team to better understand and prepare for future threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How does the Home Team intend to use such data to enhance public safety and security, particularly in the monitoring of threats?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, given that the nature of much of this data is also private, there is also a need to protect and secure the data to prevent against internal abuse of the data and against cyber attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic affecting how the Home Team’s interactions with the community might take place, it is necessary to take advantage of technology to continue to provide channels to serve the community and allow individuals to access these law enforcement services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What technology has the Home Team utilised and how has the Home Team used such technology to make its service delivery more efficient and accessible to the public?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With the use of data analytics, sensors, AI and automation, training scenarios for officers can be increasingly realistic, thereby allowing for greater preparedness of our officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As the Home Team looks to train officers in skills that are relevant across Singapore’s public sector, there is a need to train in key tech skills so as to fight crime in the cyber realm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That can take place not only within the Home Team force, but officers can be attached to relevant technology companies and startups within the private sector so as to gain relevant experience and different skillsets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What are Home Team’s plans to continue to use technology to enhance the effectiveness of the officer’s training as well as to train them in methods and expertise to tackle cybercrime?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As technological advances have increased operational capability and the range of monitoring and responses to threats, the nature of the threat towards our national security and safety has evolved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Particularly, many messaging platforms, such as Telegram, have become channels facilitating an online marketplace for illegal drugs and drug paraphernalia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Home Team needs to stay ahead of this threat by similarly taking advantage of technology to both augment and sharpen existing operational responses and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How will the Home Team deploy technology in its operations?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Last year, travellers had to navigate many different restrictions imposed by different countries.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: At last year's Global Esports Games, Singapore welcomed over 150 players and officials to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: These players and officials all stayed in a bubble.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I must admit that understanding the immigration requirements and explaining them to 40 different nations was a tedious task, but everyone understood what they needed to do – what they need to do before arrival, during their stay in Singapore and before they departed.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The global Esports Federation also conducted a post-event survey with participants and I am happy to report that participants gave an 89% satisfaction rating at the way our Immigration handled the transit of passengers.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I am glad that Singapore is slowly and cautiously opening our borders to allow more travel for work, social and other purposes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: One distinguishing feature of travel during COVID-19 is the travel rules.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Each country has its own travel restrictions, instructions and protocols to abide by.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Clearing immigration during travel amidst the pandemic can, therefore, be quite a daunting task.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: As we further open our borders, how will ICA ensure that the immigration clearance processes for travellers are smooth, seamless and safe for travellers?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Further, to me, returning to Singapore from overseas is one of the warmest feelings a Singaporean can experience.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Be it returning from work, study or simply a holiday, landing at and stepping into Changi Airport is about coming home, a place we belong.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Having a seamless entry back into one’s own country is therefore, a privilege that returning citizens enjoy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: As I listened to the songs composed and sung by the talented inmates, the lyrics spoke of their strong will, the voices sang of their resolve to be a better person for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: And I can feel the desire to turn over a new leaf.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: He shared that his biggest challenge getting back to normal life is learning to live with technology.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We take for granted the conveniences the digital world bring us today but before this man was incarcerated, there was no WiFi, no mobile phone apps – it was a totally different world.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We have seen prisons leverage technology to automate work processes and enhance operational effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has also presented challenges to prison operations and the usual in-person physical engagements and programmes for inmates, for example, visits by loved ones, rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How did Prisons overcome this or ensuring that the inmates do not lose out on what they are used to in pre-COVID-19 times?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: CNB has been effective in countering illicit drugs and drug offenders, particularly traffickers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While the drug situation in Singapore remains largely under control, the proportion of new youth abusers is concerning.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We are also starting to see a trend of youths becoming more liberal towards illicit drugs as they become more exposed to alternative lifestyles on social media.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two key trends are notably concerning that complicate matters.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, what new measures will the Home Team take to address this trend?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The National Committee on Prevention, Rehabilitation and Recidivism reported that youths who had a household member with a history of substance abuse will be more likely to abuse drugs than those who did not.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, influences from the lived and learning environment matter.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As youths spend more time with parents at home and friends as well as teachers at school, how can MHA leverage this ecosystem to identify at-risk youths for more timely intervention?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There is a much more curious attitude towards drugs, such as cannabis, and procuring e-cigarettes to vape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Despite the stringent regulation and monitoring and much success in eliminating drugs in our nation, many young people are still able to seek out suppliers via messaging platforms and obtain drugs and drug paraphernalia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While part of the battle is to keep pace and cut off the source of drugs, what initiatives will MHA be deploying to nip the problem in the bud to prevent a drug-tolerant culture from taking root in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: New psychoactive substances are being supplied and manufactured with great speed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They are concocted in makeshift labs in the region and disseminated throughout ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How can the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) be made more flexible to quickly make illegal new variants and concoctions of new psychoactive substances before they hit the Singapore market?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore has come a long way in fighting to be a drug-free nation, especially in Southeast Asia where the flow of drugs is rampant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, we cannot take our success for granted but must continue to stay vigilant in the face of greater complexities in eliminating drugs amidst the pandemic as well as the proliferation of messaging platforms.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With Telegram groups often being used to illegally advertise and supply such prohibited items, the threat has evolved because of increased internet penetration and the abundance of mobile apps that allow for encrypted communications.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This facilitates an environment where there is greater anonymity and suppliers have the ability to delete messages once the transaction is complete.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: My question, therefore is, how is the Home Team using social media to inculcate the merits of a drug-free Singapore in the minds of Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What percentage are real offenders and when they reoffend, do their offences get more serious in nature?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Is there scope to go further upstream, to work with such youths and reduce the rate of recidivism?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the recent investigations into the OCBC phishing scam, revealed that the suspected perpetrators were all youths aged 18 to 22.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: No doubt, we may see more or similar offences as a new generation increasingly becomes more tech-savvy.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even if proven guilty, given their young age and misguided talent and promise, what efforts will the Ministry undertake to deter youths from misusing technology to commit offences and ensure that those who offend are guided to more constructive use of their talents and skills?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This can start with delinquent behaviour and then evolve into involvement in drugs or gangs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Typically, where they get involved in drugs, this is the start of a downward spiral, as they may move from gateway offences like glue sniffing to starting to take drugs and eventually the stronger ones like heroin and methamphetamines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Thereafter, it is a very difficult task to break them out of the cycle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has a strong, well-known Yellow Ribbon Programme to help rehabilitate offenders and help them get back into society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, I think it is even more helpful if we can intervene at an earlier stage, say, at the first signs of delinquent behaviour, or, if possible, even before that, if it is possible to identify youths at-risk.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our relative success is fueled by the good work of our officers in MHA and its agencies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is complemented with an ecosystem of support like Yellow Ribbon Singapore, where I volunteer and other community partners.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our approach in Singapore is, indeed a whole-of-nation effort to help with the employment and employability of ex-offenders in their path away from recidivism and towards rehabilitation and reintegration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Society's perception and understanding of the challenges that ex-offenders face are crucial to our reintegration efforts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Clear efforts have to be made to remove stigmatisation and labels.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Personally, I prefer the term "overcomers" instead of "ex-offenders" as it better reflects their journey to overcome their chequered and challenging past.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, how is MHA working with other partners to support the rehabilitation and reintegration of offenders, generally, and in particular, to drug-related offences?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is MHA working with the community to strengthen support for ex-offenders?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The “Dadah Itu Haram” campaign has been around for almost five years.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And we have already seen how these efforts are effective in fostering greater awareness and reducing the number of drug offenders in our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Here, I would like to acknowledge CNB and MHA officers who have been working very hard to help save our community from the drug scourge.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their sacrifices and efforts will shape the future of our children in a life free from drugs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that more community members and organisations will answer the call and get together to assist this noble effort.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In view of these latest statistics, what are MHA's next plans and updates to cooperate with Malay/Muslim organisations on the fight against drugs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the lessons and approaches in the “Dadah Itu Haram” campaign that can be applied to reach out to other communities or young people?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: My Clementi resident came looking for help sometime back, just released from prison, nearly, 60 years old.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: When he was in Changi Prison, his medical care and follow-ups were at a hospital in the east of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But upon release home to Clementi in the west, he had a referral letter to the polyclinic listing 11 medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: He had eight medical appointments over the coming months at medical centres in the east of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Each trip for medical care and back, from west to east, would have cost him money; transport costs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: He shared he was living alone upon release from prison.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: He was on the verge of giving up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: We reached out to the healthcare teams and agencies which were able to come together and help him coordinate his medical care in the west of Singapore near Clementi.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But there will be other older Singaporeans with multiple medical conditions just released from prison trying to rebuild their lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: We know our agencies mean well, but let us continue looking at ways to improve and do even better.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY – HEAD P (MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS) (Securing our place in the world)

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The Home Team's National Servicemen work alongside a full team of full-time officers in ensuring our nation's safety and security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Some of our NSmen go on to become full-time officers after serving National Service, encouraged and inspired by their time spent serving the nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Since the pandemic, some of our NSmen have played a different but vital role in our nation's efforts to contain the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We have seen our NSmen supporting MOH's efforts in fighting COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: For example, some of our NSmen have been assisting in home vaccination efforts and the Home Recovery Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We should properly recognise their contributions and continue to ensure that every NSman's experience remains enriching.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Home Team share how it plans to further enhance the National Service experience for its National Servicemen?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our NSmen in the Home Team serve in the Police Force and SCDF.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our Home Team NS officers perform extremely important work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the years, the nature of this work has evolved, expanded, and the risks and burdens become more onerous.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope MHA can find ways to better honour, appreciate and celebrate the contributions of our Home Team NSmen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: More importantly, to stay engaged with them throughout their NS and reservist journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We have seen the Internet being abused to spread harmful misinformation about COVID-19 and vaccination and, more recently, bank-related scams.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Perpetrators who disseminate harmful content under the guise of anonymity has made it even tougher for the authorities to track them down.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Furthermore, the vastness of the Internet makes it financially burdensome for the authorities to track such content.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We must understand that platforms are intrinsically profit-driven entities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We cannot expect them to put our nation's collective interests before their business objectives.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Web3 refers to the third version of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Even though the metaverse and Web3 will provide opportunities for a better future, we should be concerned about issues of digital policies, digital identity, cybersecurity and data protection.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The metaverse and Web3 will benefit both businesses and consumer environments as well as business-to-business enterprises.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: For instance, for a manufacturer who wants to purchase equipment for spare parts, the current process involves receiving an email in two-dimensional pictures as a brochure.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: In the metaverse, there could be a virtual environment to test how the products work in a physical environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The metaverse is expected to bring more hazards to privacy, safety and security.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: There are concerns about uncivil behaviour, bullying and stalking in the mixed or virtual reality worlds.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The metaverse could also provide forums for manipulation and misinformation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Web3 is expected to bring about a paradigm shift in the way that people shop, interact socially and browse the Internet.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Web3 will focus on improving sharing of content, collective ownership and personalisation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: To ensure that citizens remain protected, can the Ministry consider updating our laws that protect Singaporeans from online harassment, identity theft and virtual crimes?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Often, those who are detained for plotting a terror attack or collaborating with overseas units to design a terror attack are misguided in their thinking and philosophy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Detaining them so as to prevent them from carrying out the act is key, but, of equal importance, is the effort to rehabilitate them such that they form their own view that violent, extreme, radical thinking manifesting in terror-plotting against the innocent is just simply incorrect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How does MHA intend to intensify its efforts in such rehabilitation and how successful has MHA been so far in rehabilitating potential terrorist threats?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Working alongside regional and global partners to combat terror and potential terror threats is key to helping prevent an incident from happening on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How will MHA continue to be a key partner in the region and, indeed, the globe, in information sharing to achieve a zero-tolerance attitude towards terrorism in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: MHA’s and its agencies’ partnership with the community to ensure radical, violent extremism does not take root in the thinking of Singaporeans is key in ensuring, pre-emptively, that the prospect of a terror attack in Singapore is minimised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How does MHA intend to intensify its collaboration with community groups to ensure that terrorism is rejected by all communities in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Home Team has served Singapore well for many years in keeping our nation safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Despite the landscape constantly changing and security threats getting increasingly complicated, the various agencies have risen to the challenge and maintained a very high standard of efficiency and having great precision in eliminating and reducing threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One aspect of the Home Team force in serving the public is protecting and partnering the community to face any obstacle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That includes how the public can contact the various departments and Statutory Boards to provide feedback or raise queries and concerns or seek help.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That also includes the day-to-day service to the community to protect them from the myriad of potential threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How can the partnership with communities and neighbourhoods be enhanced to deter crime?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Cases which involve individuals from whom debt collectors approach in their residential homes are especially troubling.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Oftentimes, in such cases, the debt collectors not only harass the debtors and their families, but also cause disamenities in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Families with seniors or young children are rightly concerned that such actions taken by debt collectors may inadvertently and potentially cause harm to them and other families living in the vicinity, even if they are not the ones in debt.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Further, as we know, over the past two years, the pandemic has caused job insecurities for Singaporeans in many industries affected by the pandemic and measures taken to protect public health.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: This could have caused some families to fall into financial hardship or exacerbate debt-related difficulties.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I, therefore, invite the Minister to share with this House whether the Government has any plans to address this issue and, if so, how do they intend to do so.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Criminals are taking advantage of more people communicating and transacting online due to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most common cases include technical support, Internet love, e-commerce, jobs, investment, loan- and bank-related phishing scams and/or China-related official impersonations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The money conned from the victims are often channelled through money mules, which allow scammers to use their bank accounts or assisted them by carrying out bank transfers and withdrawals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The security sector has seen several changes over the years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is great work by the tripartite bodies in the sector – unions, employer associations and, especially Government agencies like MHA, SPF, MOM and others.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The private security sector is a largely outsourced one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This means that other than the officers and their employers – the security agencies – there is a third stakeholder that plays a disproportionately large role in how well deployed or productive the security efforts are.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The best way to procure security is an outcome-based contracting model: to first be clear of the security objectives sought for the site through a proper analysis and audit.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is then followed by the installation of the right security technologies to harden the site before deploying the right manpower with the right skills to leverage technologies to achieve the desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Officers are tasked to man CCTV screens and manually record vehicle licence plates even today when technologies to handle such tasks are readily available at very affordable prices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This will help increase the security outcomes for the sites and also raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: A first step to consider, perhaps, is to look at how the relevant legislation can be modified to require licensed security consultants to be appointed as qualified persons of sorts, much like the construction industry, to ensure that security contracts encompass and embrace outcome-based contracting.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Unfortunately, the practice today, especially in the residential sector of the market, is still "cheap-sourcing" – based on headcount.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The operating model and mindset are still very much about having warm bodies on site to do tasks that technology can already do today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Meanwhile, existing officers in the sector put in longer hours and unsustainable shifts to plug the gap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I understand from the Union of Security Employees that split shifts with two hours in between, for example, are a common practice today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But during these two hours, the officer may very well be unable to leave the site, especially if it is in a far-flung location.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In addition, I would like to ask if MHA has other plans to uplift security officers, encourage women participation in the sector and enhance respect by society at large for the profession.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In 2021, crimes related to scams have increased significantly.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This is sizable and more than the $500 million Jobs and Business Support Package or the $560 million Household Support Package.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: If scams are not curbed safely and resolutely, coupled with the looming threat of more complex cyber crimes, our national efforts towards creating a safer digital economy may be derailed.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: While our agencies have stepped up, cases show that scammers are innovative and brazen and appear to be a step ahead.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Scam typologies consistently evolve to exploit different weaknesses along the payments value chain, testing every link of the digital ecosystem and generally, originate from overseas.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Similarly, MHA also needs to enhance cross-jurisdictional cooperation to cripple foreign scam syndicates to effectively recover lost monies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Can the Minister elaborate on MHA's strategy to foster stronger partnerships with foreign agencies?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Community engagement is equally core to SPF's crime prevention strategy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In our fight against scams, a vigilant and discerning public is the first and foremost important line of defence, as are those in the value chain such as online marketing places, telcos, fintech and banks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: On this basis, what are the Home Team's new plans to develop and deepen the engagement and set minimum standards across the payments ecosystem to defend against digital crimes?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Minister of State Desmond Tan had previously mentioned in this House that Police investigators are stretched, given more workload.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: As such, beyond an increase in manpower, we also need to equip investigators with the right cyber and commercial crime expertise.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Lastly, given the recent media reports and commentaries, can the Minister provide the Government's views on the Court of Appeals' judgment on the constitutional challenge to section 377A of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will first address Mr Derrick Goh's question about the recent Court of Appeals' judgment on the constitutional challenge to section 377A of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prime Minister Lee said in Parliament in 2007, when the Penal Code was amended but section 377A was left unchanged, that we want to be "a stable society with traditional heterosexual family values but with space for homosexuals to live their lives and to contribute to society." He added, "Among them are some of our friends, our relatives, our colleagues, our brothers and sisters or some of our children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our kith and kin." This remains our stand today.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is why we take a "live and let live" approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We seek to be an inclusive society where mutual respect and tolerance for different views and practices are paramount.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: LGBTQ+ individuals are entitled to live peacefully without being attacked or threatened.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Likewise, any attack on any other group based on their religion or religious beliefs, even if those beliefs run counter to values held by LGBTQ+ groups, will not be acceptable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, our emphasis on gradual evolution and traditional families remain constant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: However, since this issue was last discussed in Parliament in 2007, social attitudes towards homosexuality have gradually shifted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One of the things that upsets the LGBTQ+ community is that many feel that their experience of being hurt or rejected by their families, friends, schools and companies is not recognised, indeed, often denied.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, a large majority want to preserve the overall tone of our society, in particular, the traditional view of marriage as being between a man and a woman, and their children should be raised within such a family structure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their concern is not section 377A per se but the broader issues of marriage and family.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many amongst this group also support decriminalising homosexual sex between men.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Policies need to evolve to keep abreast of such changes in views and legislation needs to evolve to support updated policies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at successive Court judgments over the years, the Courts have consistently taken the position that these are highly contentious social issues and within the province of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The heterosexual stable family remains the social norm and the current legal position reflects our society's norms, values and attitudes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this latest judgment, the Court noted the compromise which Singapore has struck in respect of section 377A is unique.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach strikes a balance between preserving the legislative status quo whilst accommodating the concerns of those directly affected by the legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court recognised that the Government did this in order to avoid driving a deeper wedge within our society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also noted that Singapore's approach seeks to keep what to do with section 377A within the democratic space.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Socially charged issues such as section 377A call for continued discussion and open-ended resolution within the political domain, where we can forge consensus rather than in win-lose outcomes in Court.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this way, we can accommodate divergent interests, avoid polarisation, facilitate incremental change.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Furthermore, the Court highlighted the importance of creating space for peaceful coexistence among the various groups, especially since the balance between the various interests around section 377A has grown more delicate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These opinions align with the approach that the Government has taken in dealing with section 377A and that it intends to take as it considers the changes in our social landscape since 2007.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now move on to the rest of my Committee of Supply (COS) speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will focus on two issues – the death penalty and our approach to rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleagues from MHA will talk about MHA's plans, new capabilities, use of technology, tackling drug abuse and the fight against scams.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will mention four today: first, to deter crimes; second, to provide proportionate punishment for offenders; three, to protect public safety; and four, to rehabilitate ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How our Government balances these objectives depends on a country’s needs and values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that context, I want to talk about the death penalty, which I will call DP for short.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex A sets out the list of offences for which the DP can be imposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if the death penalty remains relevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will answer by making the following points: first, does the DP have deterrent effect; second, what is its effect on the behaviour of drug traffickers; third, Singaporeans' attitude towards the DP; fourth, specifically, what are the wider harms imposed on society by drug traffickers; and fifth, the outcomes in Singapore as a result of the approach we have taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three years before, the average was 29 cases per year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three years after, the average became one case per year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was on the rise in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of firearms offences immediately fell by 39% in 1974 to 106 cases and continued to decline in subsequent years, ever lower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Firearms offences remain very rare today in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is a historical perspective and the charts speak for themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I could go on a little bit about it, but let me just deal with a few short points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It appears to us, specifically in relation to drugs, that our position on drugs, including imposing the DP is well known in some of our neighbouring regions and that has contributed to a strong deterrent effect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA specifically commissioned a study on persons from parts of the region outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are places from where most of our arrested drug traffickers have come from in recent years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many around the world, some in Singapore, who say: "Well, why do you not replace it with life imprisonment?"; 69% in the region believe that the DP is more effective in discouraging people from committing serious crimes compared to life imprisonment; 83% believed that the DP makes people not to want to traffic substantial amount of drugs into Singapore – 83%.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I emphasise this – these are the places from which many of our traffickers come from.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You remove the death penalty, that number, 83%, will surely be reduced because there is money to be made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just go back to the second question, 69% believe that DP is more effective than life imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a fair assumption to say that more people will traffic drugs into Singapore, more drugs will enter into Singapore, there will be more drug abusers in Singapore and more Singaporean families and individuals will be harmed, if we remove the DP, in particular, the mandatory death penalty (MDP).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, those who campaign against the DP ought to answer these questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are debates we can have in society, but they ought to answer these questions and deal with them and face up to them squarely, and then debate on that basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My view is that Singaporean lives and livelihoods, a large number of that, will be at risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we have taken a tough line on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the introduction of the DP has also changed the behaviour of drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1990, the Government introduced the MDP for trafficking in more than 1.2 kilogrammes of opium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a 2018 study conducted by MHA, we found a very high level of awareness of the DP amongst convicted drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This had influenced their drug trafficking behaviour and it is consistent with the survey I spoke about earlier in the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the traffickers in this study said the following: he knew very clearly that if he were caught for trafficking a small amount, he would just go to jail for trafficking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if he was caught with a larger amount, he would be at risk of the death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And so he trafficked below the threshold amount.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked if Singaporeans continued to support the use of the DP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is my third point, the majority of Singapore residents support the use of the DP and agree that the DP deters serious crimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2019, our MHA survey showed very strong support for the DP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We conducted a follow-up survey in 2021, with a segment specifically on MDP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not just a question of survey results, whether more people agree or less people agree.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If, as policy-makers, having studied the issues and the facts, we believe this is the right thing to do, then it is our duty, both mine and Members, if you are convinced, to try and persuade people on what is the right course of action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the end, we also have to lead by persuading, explaining and if we are wrong, then the counter-arguments prevail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now move to my fourth point on the wider harm of drugs and why we take a firm stance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked how Singapore compared with countries that did not have DP for drug offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, let me answer it in a broader way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us take a look at other cities around the world, some of which have taken a softer stance on drugs and some are going or have already gone down the path of legalisation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: See the examples from the US and the UK in Annex B-1 and Annex B-2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Delaware, one of the places most affected by drug abuse in the US, more than 2,300 people have died of drug overdoses since 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is about the number of people who have also died of COVID-19 in Delaware, since the beginning of the pandemic until end of 2021.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is useful for Members to watch this video.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In many countries, including in Singapore, there is a small group who will bring out sob stories on the drug traffickers and their parents and how they should not face the penalties that the law provides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their parents will be put on display crying.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Huge numbers of babies are born in withdrawal and addiction, and these drug traffickers profit from destroying these children and their families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a snapshot, what you saw, of what it looks like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have largely not had this in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, those who ask us to abolish the death penalty should answer these questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it gets to that situation, it will be too late.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some who will say, "We are not talking about decriminalisation in Singapore".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will say our laws are already adequate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are talking only about removing the DP or MDP; keep all the other tough laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, I gave you the survey results.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Removing the DP and what impact it will have, psychologically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we have never said that the DP or MDP alone is sufficient.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is, however, a key part of our system and approach to deal with drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need many different things to keep Singapore relatively free from drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Good intelligence, strong enforcement, stiff punishments, rehabilitation for offenders, and deterrence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you heard earlier what people in the region say, what convicted drug traffickers say about the DP being a very strong deterrent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am telling Members we have to think very carefully about this before removing any part of this framework or going soft.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who advise for removal often compare us with countries which have already lost the drug war.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure if they understand the consequences or choose not to understand them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because the consequences are plain for everyone to see.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has not become less effective, it is just that we have managed to reduce the number of people who engage in drug abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a large number of people, potential abusers, whose lives have been saved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore does well in measures of safe cities, such as the Gallup survey and the Safe Cities Index.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if we change the laws, we cannot expect crime to remain low.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The tents that were in Skid Row in LA now covers many blocks, and this is what it looks like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Chairman, can I have your permission to play video three please?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not seeking to draw a direct comparison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many other reasons for homelessness in these places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But just note, the homeless also have addiction and drug abuse problems and some of that will spill over; when people cannot live with others because of drug abuse problems, they will spill out onto the streets and crime will go up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look in the UK, we see similar problems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Sheffield, for example, the drug problem has led to an increase in violent and armed crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of people dying of drug-related deaths in Sheffield has tripled between 2010 and 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, let me turn to outcomes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether there was a worsening of the drug situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of new drug abusers is higher than we would like it to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had earlier shared how the number of abusers arrested in Singapore has, over the years, gone down, and how that is also linked to low crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Drugs are not the sole cause of murders, violence or crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we look at the overseas examples, a variety of other factors shape safety in cities, including the availability of guns, how effective the criminal justice system and the police are, and many other factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in my view, drug abuse and the prevalence of drug gangs are an important contributing factor and it links up to quite a lot of other factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, by being tough on drug offences, we minimise the harms of drugs in our society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We prefer not to have to impose the DP on anyone, but we must continue to do what is best for us as a national policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked whether we would consider allowing issuance of Certificates of Substantive Assistance (CSA) to offenders when the case is before the Court of Appeal, instead of before their trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The purpose of the CSA is to encourage offenders to come clean and to provide assistance before trial, provide assistance to CNB in breaking down criminal gangs, drug gangs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is what I have to say on DP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given the time available, I have not said everything I would like to have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a tendency to think of the Singapore system as being tough.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not blame Members because I have just spent, I think the last 20 minutes or so explaining why we need to be tough on drug offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But to describe it simply as tough is not a complete and accurate descriptor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to be tough on drugs, but the complete picture, even on drugs, is not about just being tough.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are tough on those that we have to be tough on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, for example, drug abusers, we try to not even treat them as criminals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We, instead, treat their drug dependency through a variety of means.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without a criminal record, if their situation is that they are only drug abusers and have not committed any other crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And our criminal justice system has evolved quite substantially to help those who have gotten onto the wrong side.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let me talk about the different aspects of it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As part of rehabilitation, we have moved to alternate types of sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex C lists some of the types of orders which our Courts can make for minor offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts can consider these in appropriate cases, instead of traditional sentences, such as imprisonment or fine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are the: Mandatory Treatment Order (MTO), Day Reporting Order (DRO), Community Work Order (CWO), Community Service Order (CSO) and Short Detention Order (SDO).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about our efforts to improve the employability of inmates and our work with the community in bringing down recidivism rates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is one of the lowest for comparable cities around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has gone down a little bit over the years, but we want to try and bring it down further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some factors that can lead to a successful reintegration in the long term.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These include stable employment, positive pro-social networks and personal motivation to seek help and contribute to society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When inmates are admitted to prison, they have their risks and needs identified and undergo appropriate programmes to address them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are four broad areas: one, psychology-based correctional programmes; two, family programmes; three, skills training and employment assistance; and four, community corrections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under psychology-based correctional programmes, correctional rehabilitation specialists and psychologists do intervention programmes for inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates may have rehabilitation needs, including relating to substance abuse, anti-social attitudes, interpersonal violence, sexual violence and other mental health needs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, our experts will look at these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second aspect is working with the family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Strong family support is essential in the rehabilitation and re-integration journey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisons conducts programmes, social skills training programme and the Family Reintegration Programme (FRP).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The aim is to help the inmates link up, bond with their family, strengthen the bonds with their family and loved ones.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisons also works with community partners, for example, Centre for Fathering, The Salvation Army and New Life Stories, to facilitate family bonding programmes for inmates and their children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some families may also face difficulties during the inmates’ incarceration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisons proactively refers families of inmates who require assistance to Family Service Centres.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the broader community, grassroots volunteers are roped in to support families impacted by incarceration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
