text: Third is the Skills Training and Employment Assistance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Having a stable job upon release reduces the risk of re-offending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Mark Chay asked about the success of the Train and Place (TAP) and Grow Initiative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The TAP and Grow initiative works on equipping inmates with skills to secure and sustain jobs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also asked if there are plans to expand this initiative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can go for academic programmes while in prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Programmes range from GCE to diploma and degree programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the TAP and Grow initiative, training academies in prison have been set up in partnership with the media, precision engineering and logistics sectors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates will be offered jobs by the partner employers upon release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Twenty-eight inmates completed the training and graduated with diplomas in media courses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This year, YRSG does aim to make the initiative bigger and go into the food services sector.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: YRSG has also developed a digital literacy masterplan for inmates to gain basic digital skills in prison so that they are better prepared for the job market upon release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An estimated 750 inmates will be trained in basic digital skills each year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: YRSG has also partnered IMDA to roll out digital skills training for older residents at the Selarang Halfway House and this training helps with digital services, including Government services and financial services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fourth aspect I want to mention is community corrections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Research has shown that there are better rehabilitation outcomes when rehabilitation in prison is complemented by community-based programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Results from community corrections continue to be encouraging.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2021, close to 90% of the inmates who were placed on community-based programmes completed them successfully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates who have completed these programmes have a lower risk of reoffending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisons is also developing a Digitalised Learning and Support Package for inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The aim is to better prepare inmates for their emplacement in the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The efforts I have described will not be effective if the community is not willing to give ex-offenders a second chance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: YRSG helps with our reintegration efforts and my colleague, Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim, will speak about this later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera then reprised a part of the FICA debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At that time, I pointed out to him that, in Singapore, we take investigations very seriously and I explained how the system works and that the Prime Minister can be the subject of independent investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He did not respond then, but he has come back to it today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is wrongdoing by anyone, whether a Minister or civil servant or private sector person, there will be investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, over the years, we have added on the checks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Government has added on checks on itself, which are very rare elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We institutionalised it such that the CPIB can go straight to the Prime Minister but, where the Prime Minister himself is the possible subject of investigations, or if the Prime Minister does not want to do something, the CPIB can go to the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, I will come back to this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, if there is any wrongdoing or suspected wrongdoing, known to anyone, including suspicion of foreign interference or influence, you can let CPIB know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CPIB has the resources to carry out the investigations and it has the ability to tap onto other agencies for the appropriate additional help or work that needs to be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And FICA put in place a framework where interactions cross the line and you become the subject of foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is a legal basis to act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera's suggestion, if I understood him correctly, is that why not we set up a separate ombudsman with the resources to carry out all these investigations?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because he had a question about whether the CPIB was adequately resourced, trained, does it have the ability to handle these matters?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, my inference from that way of phrasing the question is, therefore the agency, whichever agency is set up, must replicate, I suppose, many parts of our law enforcement agencies, including our intel agencies, so that they can do this on a standalone basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you only have the ombudsman without this apparatus that I have described, then he or she will go to the law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, in such a situation, the law enforcement agencies can go to the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is an independent person who can give the directions and who can authorise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, Mr Leon Perera referred to New Zealand and I have often found that, we make these references – they sound sexy, but then, when you actually look at what is happening, I find that the debates get very academic, without any grounding in reality, without perhaps either understanding or acknowledging what really happens in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is our situation – how well we have managed to handle and keep corruption low and official wrongdoing low and how other countries are in this context?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The country's Minister for Justice Andrew Little admitted last month, like many democracies around the world, ours is vulnerable to those abroad who would seek to interfere in our democratic processes and influence the outcome." I am not going to read the whole article.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will make it available to Members or I will give the reference in a while.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New Zealand's National Party Member of Parliament Todd McClay was featured in a report by Freedom House as an example of how they say which foreign government forges relationships with foreign politicians who promote a certain view in local media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The country's new legislation on electoral funding did not include changes to this massive loophole.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2016, New Zealand was described as "at the heart" of global money laundering.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The ease for foreigners to set up a company in the country is one of the reasons why money launderers have been attracted to do business there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You would think New Zealand's other political parties would be making hay with all this material, but they have been mute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would ask Members to perhaps do their research before they cite various countries and their institutions as models.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, here we have an elected Government, which has to govern, and I will come back to this point and explain it a bit later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, let me ask, you set up an ombudsman with or without the full suite of resources and without any oversight from the Government, who then deals with misconduct by the ombudsman or the officers within that office?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera said during the FICA debate "quis custodiet ipsos custodes?", if I recall correctly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For some reason, I think that phrase seems to have lost favour now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take a hypothetical situation: say, you have an organisation, where the top leaders engage in wrongdoing or, for example, say, they set up a disciplinary committee to cover up what they did rather than actually investigate, I think you can ask "quis custodiet ipsos custodes?".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And these civil servants are protected through the structure of Public Service Commission, which, in turn, is protected through the fact that appointment cannot be interfered with willy-nilly by the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you take the senior appointments, including the chief of CPIB, Chief Justice, Attorney-General – all these – there are carefully constructed structures on these appointments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I would say, look at all that first and look at the ground situation before we start talking about replicating more and more institutions outside.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In contrast, look at countries with a longer runway of democracy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Australia – I stand corrected – but in the short time I had since Mr Leon Perera spoke, the example I found is Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), a state-level agency that reports to the premier; in this case, the case that was highlighted to me, the Prime Minister of New South Wales.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at what is the situation in the UK – I am reading from something that says "Institute for Government – Ministerial Code", what does the Code say?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of the Codes, meaning the Codes for Wales, Scotland and UK, give the final authority for decisions about action to be taken to the Prime Minister or First Minister or, in Northern Ireland, the relevant nominating officer for a particular Minister's party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since 2006, UK Government Ministerial Code breaches have been investigated through an independent adviser on ministerial interest or by the cabinet secretary, but there is no requirement to follow any particular process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think the Member will be well aware of the situation in the UK more recently and for some period in the recent past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, a second question on caning and whether there was a requirement for those who have been caned to thank the officers after the caning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he has suggested there should be – no surprises – an outside commission to decide on institutional caning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the years, I have listened to the speeches, Mr Leon Perera, in particular.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In FICA, there was a suggestion of ombudsman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think these are the things on which there can be positive contributions, and my Ministry will always be open to positive contributions, regardless of who it comes from, whether people in this Chamber, whether from the Government or Opposition, or members of public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is possible to implement it, we will implement it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2015, MHA started our ambitious Home Team Transformation Journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We recognised the need to overhaul the Home Team’s operational model to ensure we would be future-ready to meet evolving challenges, as new threats emerge amidst higher public expectations, rising workload and manpower constraints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Seven years on, we have seen encouraging results.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the 2020 edition of the Home Team Public Perception Survey, over 88% of the respondents agreed that the Home Team uses technology effectively to enhance Singapore’s safety and security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the era of hyper-innovation, each successful adoption of technology is merely the beginning of more to come.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will update Members on our efforts in three areas: first, new capabilities for greater operational effectiveness; second, safer and more convenient services for the public; and, third, upskilling of our officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza said as the nature of threats evolve, the Home Team needs to stay ahead by using technology to augment our operational responses and capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Public trust is built on our ability to detect and prevent threats, and our speed of incident response.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Vikram Nair asked about the Police Cameras.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fortunately, we are operating from a position of strength.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In a survey conducted by SPF in 2021, 91% of respondents supported the installation of Police Cameras in public areas to deter, detect and solve crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SPF will continue to expand the cameras’ coverage to more public spaces and heartland areas to improve our response against crime and security threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The footage from these cameras is stored securely and only accessed by authorised officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is applied to help officers analyse the high-volume of footage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SCDF has also been enhancing its capability over the years to better detect hazardous materials.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the next few years, SCDF will implement a real-time 24/7 nationwide sensor grid to enable early detection of hazardous materials.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With earlier detection, SCDF will be able to quickly dispatch resources to investigate and manage the situation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The management of an incident involving hazardous materials is time critical, as these substances pose significant risks to public health property and the environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are also using technology, so that officers can respond faster and better to incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SPF and SCDF will be enhancing their 999 and 995 operation centres with VEEN, or Video Extension for Emergency Numbers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: VEEN will allow officers in the Ops Centre to initiate a video call on the mobile phone of the 999 or 995 caller.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With that, the Ops Centre will be able to see what is happening on the ground and officers arriving at the scene will be able to react quicker and better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SCDF frontline officers will also be equipped with smart devices, such as smart phones, tablets and smart watches, so that they can respond better in emergencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: An example would be OMNII, or the Operational Medical Networks Informatics Integrator, jointly developed by SCDF and MOH.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Launched in mid-2021, OMNII helps paramedics to make better interventions when responding to emergency medical cases through accessing a patient’s relevant medical data on the go.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Paramedics can also quickly share information with the hospitals, so that the patient can receive timely assistance upon arrival.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second area I will speak about is how we use technology to improve service delivery to the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the COVID-19 pandemic, we have accelerated the digitalisation of our services to minimise physical touch points and to reach more Singaporeans safely and conveniently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, the majority of ICA’s transactional e-services see a high take-up rate of over 80%.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This year, ICA will make available more digital documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members of the public will soon be able to apply for and access documents digitally, such as birth and death certificates, long-term visit passes and student passes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This makes these processes completely digital end-to-end, and we will no longer need to worry about losing such important documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This also saves time spent on travelling and collecting physical documents at ICA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Identity cards and passports will remain physical documents as current legislation still requires the presentation of physical identity cards in certain settings and we need to adhere to international passport standards set out by the International Civil Aviation Organisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In time to come, these digital documents can be securely and conveniently retrieved on our mobile devices through the “MyICA Mobile” app.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA will also be making more e-services, such as the application of identity cards, passports and extension of visit passes available on this app.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Mark Chay asked how technology can assist in the safe reopening of Singapore’s borders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As international travel starts to open up, we expect the number of travellers passing through our checkpoints to increase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the longer term, most residents, long-term pass holders and visitors will be cleared through automated lanes in the passenger halls, which will be faster, more efficient and more secure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All lanes can be flexibly allocated to serve specific traveller groups according to operational needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng asked how we have used technology to facilitate rehabilitation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have used technology to ensure our rehabilitation programmes can continue during the pandemic and keep families close to inmates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through the virtual family programmes, inmates were able to connect with their children, despite the pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SPS also partnered Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG) to facilitate virtual job placement interviews, allowing inmates to continue to access employment assistance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These virtual initiatives will be kept up to complement in-person sessions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SPS also uses tablets to facilitate inmates’ rehabilitation with self-directed learning and engagement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Inmates connect with their families and friends through e-letters and keep up with the news.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This sense of connection with their loved ones and society is essential to their rehabilitation process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A third and important area is the use of technology to make training safer and more realistic for our officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One example is SPF’s Live Instrumentation Training System, which does away with the need for our officers to fire live rounds during simulated tactical trainings; instead, lasers and body-worn detectors are used.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To make taser training safer for our officers, the Mobile TASER Training Target system uses computer vision technology to detect and analyse data, such as where the taser probes are targeted at, thus removing the need for conventional methods where officers wearing protective suits serve as targets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They, too, want to have a stake in better understanding and leveraging technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Thus, each Home Team Department has developed their own digital upskilling roadmaps to equip their officers with the relevant digital skills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team is also using technology to train our officers to tackle cyber crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we equip our Home Team officers with tools to detect and provide intelligence on cyber crime activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) developed an E-Commerce Surveillance Tool that uses AI to help enforcement officers sift through online listings of contrabands.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As data mining and analysis are fully automated, this significantly reduces the enforcement efforts of contraband items from days or even weeks to a matter of hours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we train and keep our officers updated on the latest cyber crime trends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, SPF works with private sector organisations to train officers on technology features and technical skills to combat cyber crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA will build key capabilities to enable the delivery of our future digitalisation initiatives and accelerate innovation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: HEIDI will enable HTX to quickly adopt and create new digital capabilities so that capacity can be scaled up quickly to meet future needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will also provide enhanced data security and stronger operational control compared to regular commercial cloud services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With HEIDI, the Home Team will be in a stronger position to fulfil our mission.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will press on to ensure that Singapore remains a safe and secure home for all of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prevention and rehabilitation play an important role in our successes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about our efforts to identify and work with those who are at-risk of offending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah asked about MHA's efforts to prevent young individuals from offending and re-offending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Police and the National Crime Prevention Council have been jointly organising the Delta League since 2011.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We engage youths through football tournaments, workshops and e-sports to imbue a sense of teamwork, discipline and social responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We piloted the Localised Community Network (LCN) in 2019 to provide support for children and youths who exhibit at-risk behaviours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Programme (YGP) has been in place since 2012 and engages around 300 youths each month through structured activities to reduce risky behaviour, build positive relationships and life skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah asked about the percentage of youths who re-offend.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We do not track if these youths' subsequent offences become more serious in nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Apart from upstream efforts, we also invest in rehabilitation and reintegration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Minister Shanmugam has spoken about rehabilitation in his speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our rehabilitation efforts would not be effective if the community is not willing to give ex-offenders a second chance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked how we can improve job search prospects for ex-offenders and further incentivise HR practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Hiring ex-offenders is one of the most symbolic acts of acceptance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Yellow Ribbon Singapore, or YRSG, has built a system of support to incentivise, recognise and empower employers to hire ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Placement exercises are held in prison to match inmates with suitable employers prior to release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For up to 12 months, career coaches work with ex-offenders and their employers to set behavioural goals and resolve work issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Later this year, YRSG will launch the Friends of Yellow Ribbon network to galvanise individuals, community groups and employers to advance second chances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Currently, about 80% of ex-offenders assisted by YRSG are employed in lower-wage jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOM will implement the Progressive Wage Mark, or PW Mark, to accredit firms that pay progressive wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Beyond employers, YRSG has put in place a community action masterplan to map out opportunities for the community to be involved and better harness the strengths and aspirations of volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons partners community organisations and volunteers to provide pro-social support to ex-offenders when they are released into the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under the Throughcare Volunteer Framework, or TVF, volunteers involve them in activities after their release and connect them to wider communities of support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2021, all 11 religious partners working with Prisons adopted the TVF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We are heartened by the strong support of prison volunteers and community partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: On the drug front, the local drug situation remains under control.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Among them is the observation that there is a gradual slide towards increasingly liberal attitudes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To better protect Singapore from the scourge of drugs, we will strengthen the three pillars of our harm prevention efforts: tough laws and robust enforcement; preventive drug education or PDE; and rehabilitation and aftercare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We intend to amend the Misuse of Drugs Act to better regulate new psychoactive substances, expand PDE efforts to forge a national consensus of zero tolerance against drugs and enhance drug supervision to support former abusers in leading drug-free lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, Mr Christopher de Souza asked how the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) could be made more flexible to deal with new variants of new psychoactive substances, or NPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MHA will amend the MDA to introduce a new legislative framework to regulate NPS, based on their potential to produce a psychoactive effect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will allow us to be more responsive to emerging forms of NPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked how we address the use of the digital space for dealing in drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB will continue with operations targeting trafficking and abusers who use encrypted messaging applications such as Telegram.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Derrick Goh asked how we address liberalising attitudes towards drugs and strengthen resilience for a drug-free Singapore, especially among youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about the impact of our efforts in spreading the anti-drug message.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB has been leveraging social media to secure mindshare to build a drug-free Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In May 2021, CNB released the short film "Down The Rabbit Hole".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The film sheds light on the mercenary motivations of drug pushers and traffickers who had profited at the expense of vulnerable and addicted persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To involve parents and educators of youths, CNB published an information booklet on "Staying Free from New Psychoactive Substances".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This booklet provides tips on identifying tell-tale signs that their children are abusing drugs and ways to help youths stay away from drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In fact, if you go to the CNB website, you will be able to see many resources and information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also engage in using social media, such as Instagram and Facebook.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Whenever there are arrests, we also share such photos so that we can get people aware and involved in such efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: So, I hope you can support us and share our messages and issues that we want to proactively reach out to Singaporeans with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB also organises an annual video competition to provide a platform to engage older youths interested in video production.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This allows youths to articulate their understanding of the harms of drugs and promote anti-drug messages through short videos.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This year, CNB will reach out to more students through pre-competition workshops and provide opportunities for collaboration with CNB to develop PDE resources for their peers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am heartened that a Home Team Public Perception Survey conducted in 2020 found that more than nine in 10 respondents below the age of 30 were aware of PDE efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to engage our people to forge a strong national consensus of zero tolerance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked how MHA is working with the community to strengthen support for drug offenders and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I had earlier spoken about efforts to support the reintegration of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Former drug abusers will be subjected to supervision by CNB to support them in leading drug-free lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB will be enhancing its drug supervision scheme to better support the reintegration of former drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since 2019, CNB has been piloting Community Supervision Skills (CoSS) sessions where CNB supervision officers will check in on supervisees and assess their residual reintegration needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke on the mixing of ex-abusers who are reporting for supervision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Currently, there are different reporting days for youth and adult supervisees to prevent undesirable interactions and contamination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Further, supervisees are not allowed to communicate with each other during reporting and are to leave the reporting centre once they are done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will now speak in Malay on the supportive role played by the Malay/Muslim community in our fight against drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Zhulkarnain requested an update on MHA's collaboration with the Malay/Muslim community in the fight against drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These include Malay/Muslim organisations, such as FITRAH, PERGAS and AMP, which provide intervention and outreach programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to support other Malay/Muslim organisations to build upon and expand the network.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The "Dadah Itu Haram" campaign has been going on for almost five years with the aim of working with the Malay/Muslim community to spread the message of living healthy, drug-free lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To ensure continued participation during COVID-19, CNB conducted more than 20 virtual and hybrid events in 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2021, all 71 mosques across Singapore participated in the International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking for the first time by displaying "Dadah Itu Haram" signages and banners in the mosque compounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This event included a Friday sermon specially prepared by MUIS on the importance of prohibiting drug abuse and to raise awareness about the dangers of drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The latest survey on the "Dadah Itu Haram" campaign is very encouraging.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It shows the community’s strong support towards this campaign and there is encouraging evidence of this campaign’s success in spreading the anti-drug message to the target group within the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We are studying the “Dadah Itu Haram” campaign to identify the learning points that can be used to increase our reach to other groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We thank the community for their support in the war against drugs, and we look forward to more collaborations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In English): Sir, I will now address Dr Tan Wu Meng's question on ensuring proper handover of medical care for ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In general, ex-offenders who need further follow-up after release will be referred to Changi General Hospital's specialist clinics for continuity of care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons is exploring with SingHealth on facilitating follow-up appointments at other public healthcare institutions which are closer to the ex-offender's home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Before I end, I want to highlight a special group of people, namely, our National Servicemen, or NSmen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our NSmen serve alongside our regular officers with the same dedication and commitment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked about our plans to enhance the NS experience and Mr Patrick Tay asked what more could be done for our Home Team NSmen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Chairman, I will elaborate on three areas that our Home Team will be focusing on, in our partnership with the community and the industry stakeholders in the year 2022 to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These three areas are crime prevention, combatting scams and anti-terrorism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, we will continue to work with the community to prevent crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the Police’s partnerships with the community to create safer neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This scheme actually integrates the existing groups, such as the Neighbourhood Watch Zone (NWZ), Vehicles on Watch and Riders on Watch, into an overall community partnership programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some members have also gone beyond and to help to patrol the streets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some do so on Citizens on Patrol (COP) by donning a vest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Others go even further to don a uniform, under the Volunteer Special Constabulary scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These efforts have helped make our neighbourhoods and communities safer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One example I would like to highlight is Mr Pragash s/o Kulasagar, who has volunteered via the COP scheme for 20 years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In February 2018, while on patrol, Mr Pragash and his team were approached by a couple who shared that their domestic helper had been molested outside the lift of their flat.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Pragash and his team used the description provided and were able to narrow down the identity of culprit and helped solved the crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked how the Government will tackle public disorder and disamenities brought about by errant debt collection activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, on our whole-of-society approach to tackling scams and cheating cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Derrick Goh and Mr Mark Chay asked how the Government will combat the scourge of scams together with our stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In February, I made a Ministerial Statement on two aspects of our approach: (a) enforcement; and (b) public education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I mentioned about the Anti-Scam Centre, which continues to be effective and will continue to be organised for better effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I talked about working with transnational agencies and jurisdictions and law enforcement agencies to continue to be more effective as many of these crimes were transboundary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And finally, we will continue to work with the telcos as well as the banks to secure our network and to ensure that our funds are secure in the transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some of the measures, including blocking of SMSes, phone calls as well as websites, will be introduced in the year ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will continue to explore other strategies to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This rating will help consumers understand the safety features offered by different e-marketplaces, so that they can make an informed choice on where or how they are going to do their online shopping.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are also working with agencies to develop a framework that will help us tackle scams as well as a broader suite of criminal activity online, such as child pornography, terrorism and content inciting violence in our communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ultimately, we want a safer online environment for all users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will engage the relevant stakeholders on our proposals very soon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is in response to Mr Desmond Choo as well as Mr Mark Chay’s questions on how we are going to deal with harmful online content and virtual crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD) is adequately resourced and whether CAD can tap on the private sector to enhance its operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As I mentioned earlier, resourcing across the SPF – that includes CAD – is indeed, very stretched.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will have to discuss with MOF on how we can increase our manpower in the Police Force to enable our forces to cope better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We regularly review the salaries of our CAD officers to make sure that they are kept competitive and are able to be adjusted should market forces also move.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Even so, this has not prevented CAD from being an effective unit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: CAD has also proactively engaged industry stakeholders to streamline its operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, in 2021, CAD worked with trusted industry partners to disrupt an extensive network of shell companies potentially used for money laundering.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This partnership allowed CAD to intercept over US$33 million in criminal proceeds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With regard to the Member’s suggestion of a whistle-blowing legislation, today, our current laws already protect the identities of informants for organised crime and money laundering offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At the same time, we take a stern view of such crimes and so our laws do not protect them from prosecution or to provide further incentives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While we can understand that whistle-blowing will encourage more people to step forward to help detection, there are also other considerations that we need to consider.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Including how it may create a moral hazard or lead to frivolous reporting, or there may be some cases where the whistle-blower themselves are complicit in the crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These consideration will have to be weighed against some of the benefits that the Member talked about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Don Wee asked how we will address “money mules” – individuals who receive and transfer tainted funds as part of a trans-national syndicated money-laundering process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, a large proportion of investigations into money mules do not result in prosecutions, due to the inherent difficulties in proving the money mule’s intent to participate in moving monies for scam syndicates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, let me touch on our approach to anti-terrorism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the Government's partnership to prevent terrorism and strengthen our response.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Key to Singapore’s counter-terrorism strategy is working closely with global security, intelligence and law enforcement agencies to foil terror attacks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, in 2016, ISD worked closely with our Indonesian counterparts to thwart a plot by the pro-Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS) group that targeted Marina Bay Sands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Government also works closely with our community and religious leaders to address the roots of the ideology upstream.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are also ramping up our community response and mobilisation capabilities against terror attacks through the SGSecure Movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked how we rehabilitate radicalised individuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, we have extensive partnerships with organisations, such as the Religious Rehabilitation Group (RRG) and the Inter-Agency Aftercare Group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To-date, over 80% of those that are detained for terrorism-related conduct have been released from detention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Most of them are gainfully employed and some are pursuing their education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They have good social support and remain resilient against radical influences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Following extensive engagement by rehabilitation stakeholders, “Daniel” has renounced his support for ISIS and his radical ideologies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While in detention, he received weekly tutoring from RRG members who are also MOE-trained teachers, to prepare him for his GCE “N” level exams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He did very well in his exams, and his achievements have strengthened his resolve to change for the better. “Daniel” has since been released from detention in January 2022 and is now furthering his education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our partners in the security industry also play a critical role in keeping Singapore safe from terrorism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Xie Yao Quan asked about the Government's role in helping this sector to be better equipped to play this role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will also uplift wages for all security officers, including women, whom we always try to recruit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since May 2020, all Government Procurement Entities are required to adopt outcome-based contracts (OBCs) for their security services and we will move towards 100% adoption of OBCs in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We hope more private sector entities will follow suit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Chairman, to conclude, let me speak a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, it is the responsibility of every Singaporean to protect Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Although we are doing our best to plan and prevent crime, it is hard to totally prevent it from happening.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We must take a three-pronged approach to curbing crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, we continue to strengthen cooperation with community partners to provide timely assistance to individuals and families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, strengthen the awareness of fraud prevention, so that scammers do not take advantage of it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Third, we must heighten vigilance against extreme anti-social attitudes and practices that create division.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the coming year, the Government and the Home Team hope to continue to work with Singaporeans to prevent and combat crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is important to be vigilant and report suspicious persons or show concern for our neighbours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Each of us can contribute to crime prevention and work together to build a Singapore where we can all live and work in peace and contentment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, as the security environment continues to evolve, the Home Team will continue to work with our community to build a safer and more secure Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: He mentioned that he was not surprised at my suggestion of a judicial check on the administration of punishments in prison.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am equally unsurprised at his disagreement with that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: He referred to New Zealand and he pointed out many problems that New Zealand has recently been grappling with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There is no doubt in my mind that if I had cited another country, he would point out problems with that country as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I made a long speech, which I do not intend to and I cannot anyway repeat, in September 2020 when I gave detailed arguments for an ombudsman, I addressed the objections to the idea, one by one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I talked about the countries that have that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And if you were to go to opinion leaders, and if you were to conduct public opinion polls in those countries, I am not at all sure that the majority of people would say that, "Well, this is a bad thing, let us remove this institution and then things will get better".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, when it investigates alleged abuses, it is seen to be an investigation coming from a different part of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think being seen to be that, to do that, has advantages in terms of vertical accountability, that is felt by the society and that has advantages in terms of the strength and solidarity of our polity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would say that there are tangible advantages to be gained from that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is difficult to speak of practical benefits that would come from instituting this proposal because it is hypothetical, of course.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Perera, if we can keep it to clarifications and questions; if we can.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I will just wrap up in the next one minute.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because I would not know what sort of cases would be referred to that, how those cases will be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What I can say is that in terms of the perception of legitimacy, I think there is a benefit there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Minister mentioned various practical issues that could come about, for example, do we want to duplicate resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I mean, there are practical solutions to that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: You could design an office ombudsman to address that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For example, investigations could be directed by the office but they could seek resources from other agencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I think for the sake of length, I will leave it at that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a way, I am not sure that we are that far apart because I had anticipated this point, which is why I said that there are two possible ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is you replicate the entire resources, that means you have various parts of the Government machinery outside which makes no sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The alternate is the ombudsman uses the Government machinery.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Perera overlooks – if he uses the machinery, those machineries sit within the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I do not understand what the argument is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Maybe Mr Perera has not understood the constitutional structure and how the CPIB can go direct to the President.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, I did not file a cut for this Ministry but in view of some of the earlier remarks made by the Minister, I have two clarifications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I just need to be sure that both were surveys; the first one covered the mandatory death penalty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If I heard the Minister right, he said the Ministry is studying the results.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And then, thereafter, Minister went on to say that in the case, for example, for intentional murder, 81% approved of the mandatory death penalty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think there were three other statistics that he revealed in that part.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I just confirm then what is the Ministry studying with regard to the mandatory death penalty for this particular survey?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to the first survey the Minister referred to, which covered foreigners in countries, I understand the Minister said where some of these drug offenders originate from.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm that that survey would be made public and not for its own sake but at least people can understand the argument vis-a-vis deterrence quite squarely and also understand the structure of the survey itself?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because people may have differing views on death penalty and mandatory death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have been given these figures with a reasonable degree of confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When it is finalised, we will make it available, we will make it public, as we have made public previous surveys.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will just take the appropriate time and we will release it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The first clarification has to do with the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Minister of State Faishal Ibrahim had mentioned that in order to make the Misuse of Drugs Act more flexible, in order to catch quickly and swiftly new psychoactive substances that come onto the market, they are looking at a framework that concentrates on the effect of the drug.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think that is a good move, but I would like to confirm with him that even if we were to go in that direction, which would make the MDA swifter, we would still retain the First Schedule which lists all the controlled drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And if you possess, deal in or consume any of those controlled drugs in the First Schedule, you will still be up for an offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, the deterrent effect on the controlled drugs remains.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: My second clarification arises out of what Minister of State Desmond Tan said on anti-terror capabilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: My question to him and my cut were really directed at what intelligence cooperation we can have across jurisdictions to ensure that there is information sharing to pre-empt a terror attack from happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And I had in mind collaborations with Interpol.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would he be able to confirm that MHA does work with organisations like Interpol to create a good intelligence environment to deter terrorist threats?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The third clarification, Sir, really arises from the Minister's position on the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: First, I want to say that it takes a lot of courage to come out and say that, because of the wave of liberal attitudes towards consumption of drugs in the globe today and in the region.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And I want to say that as a lawmaker, it is one of the toughest decisions that I have to make for my country whenever the Misuse of Drugs act comes up, if not the toughest and I have searched my conscience and I am fully in favour of the retention of the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because 15 grammes of diamorphine – heroin – feed 180 drug abusers a week.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr de Souza, can we just keep it to the question and clarification?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, my position here is that in preserving the death penalty, would MHA also share statistics about the effect of the drug and how it creates cross-generational detriment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A hundred and eighty families are one whole HDB block.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And share the empirical evidence of how the death penalty does, in fact, deter?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I just want to place on record my thanks to the Minister for going deep into a very sensitive topic notwithstanding the forces at work in the opposite direction.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr de Souza, if you can just wrap up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That is what I wanted to say and I say that as a matter of principle and conviction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Yes, indeed, we will retain the First Schedule of the MDA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Just a quick response to Mr Christopher de Souza.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In my response, I did mention that the Police as well as our intelligence agencies do work very closely with our regional, as well as extra-regional partners from the other countries to ensure there is exchange of information, there is capacity building and there are also joint operations, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, this is something that we have been working on and that includes our partnership with Interpol.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I have cited examples where we have also worked with Indonesian agencies some time ago to thwart the plot that was planned against Marina Bay Sands.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Murali Pillai, would you like to withdraw your amendment, please?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, with your leave, I would like to convey my appreciation to three groups of people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: First, the hon Members for filing 40 cuts which led to a very involved debate on issues that affect MHA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second, to the two hon Ministers and the two hon Ministers of State for their comprehensive responses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And I cannot remember another COS debate with slides and videos, and for hon Members who have seen the videos, it would probably forever be etched in their memories the pernicious effects of drugs, especially on those who are voiceless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Last but not least, on behalf of Members who spoke, I would like to record our appreciation to the Home Team officers who work every day to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With that, may I seek leave to withdraw the amendment.
